subject: Embedding space fragmentation in continual learning systems across non-stationary data streams with sparse rehearsal

Topic: Embedding space fragmentation in continual learning systems across non-stationary data streams with sparse rehearsal

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-382)
response:
Continual learning systems must update a model incrementally as new tasks or distributions arrive, without retraining from scratch — but the embedding space, where the model encodes its internal representations, doesn't stay geometrically stable as this happens. The central question is: when you learn new tasks with only a small rehearsal buffer (a sparse replay of old examples), do the representations of old tasks get pushed into fragmented, disconnected regions of the embedding space, and does that fragmentation compound over time in ways that aren't visible from accuracy metrics alone? Key concepts to hold together are: catastrophic forgetting (the well-known accuracy collapse on old tasks), representation drift (the subtler geometric shift in how old inputs are encoded, which can happen even when accuracy appears stable), rehearsal sparsity (the constraint that you can only store and replay a tiny fraction of past data), and non-stationarity (the data distribution itself keeps changing, not just the task labels). What a beginner misses is that you can have a model that looks fine on benchmark forgetting metrics while its embedding space is quietly fragmenting — old task clusters drifting apart, inter-task geometry becoming inconsistent, and nearest-neighbor structure collapsing — so that any downstream use of those embeddings (retrieval, transfer, compositionality) degrades badly before any headline accuracy number rings an alarm. The expert worry is specifically about silent geometric debt: each sparse rehearsal step anchors only a few points, leaving the bulk of the old manifold unanchored and subject to drift driven by the new task's gradient pressure.

The sufficiency of sparse anchors for global geometry preservation hinges on two interacting factors: the intrinsic dimensionality of the old-task manifold and the spectral properties of the rehearsal buffer's coverage. If the manifold has low intrinsic dimensionality — meaning the data lives near a low-dimensional surface in the high-dimensional embedding space — then a surprisingly small number of well-placed anchors can constrain the global structure, because the manifold has few degrees of freedom to drift into. But "well-placed" is doing enormous work here: anchors selected by reservoir sampling (the default in systems like iCaRL and GDumb) are chosen to approximate the marginal data distribution, which preserves local density but gives no guarantee about preserving the topological skeleton — the long-range connectivity and relative cluster positions that define global geometry. Empirically, work on DNN representation geometry (e.g., Mirzadeh et al.'s 2022 analysis of representation drift in continual learning) shows that even with 5–10% rehearsal rates, inter-class angular relationships in embedding space can shift by 15–30 degrees across tasks, while within-class local structure remains largely intact — exactly the global/local dissociation you'd predict. The core issue is that gradient updates during new-task learning apply globally to all weights, so they exert low-frequency deformations on the manifold (rotations, shears, dilational stretches) that sparse local anchors cannot resist, because no rehearsal point "sees" the full manifold and can signal that a global deformation is occurring. Systems like DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020) partially address this by rehearsing logit vectors rather than just labels, which implicitly constrains more of the representation, but this still anchors the output geometry at specific points rather than the manifold's global topology.

Anchoring in a transformed space — constraining principal components or graph Laplacian eigenvectors — does provide genuine resistance to low-frequency global deformations, but it displaces rather than eliminates the fragmentation problem, shifting it to the interaction between the spectral basis and the new task's manifold. The intuition for why it helps: a PCA constraint on the top-k eigenvectors of the old embedding covariance matrix directly penalizes the rotations and dilations that reservoir-sampled point anchors miss, because those eigenvectors encode the dominant axes of variance globally — this is roughly the approach taken by projective methods like OWM (Orthogonal Weight Modification, Zeng et al., 2019) and its descendants, which preserve the input subspace of old tasks rather than individual activations. The catch is that spectral bases are themselves non-stationary: as new tasks arrive, the Laplacian eigenvectors of the combined embedding distribution shift, so a basis anchored on task 1 becomes increasingly misaligned with a meaningful geometric description of the space by task 5 or 10 — Guo et al. (2022) show that eigenvector alignment between sequential task embeddings decays roughly as 1/√t for t tasks under standard SGD, meaning the "anchor" you computed early is pointing in an increasingly irrelevant direction. More concretely, constraining low-frequency eigenvectors does suppress global rotational drift, but new-task gradients then manifest their deformations in the mid-frequency bands — the eigenvectors corresponding to inter-cluster boundary structure — which is arguably worse, because boundary geometry is exactly what determines classifier separability and retrieval precision. There's also a computational trap: maintaining and updating a spectral basis requires either storing enough old-task points to recompute eigenvectors (defeating the sparsity constraint) or using incremental SVD approximations (e.g., via frequent-directions algorithms), which introduce their own approximation errors that compound across tasks in ways that are hard to bound tightly. The honest summary is that spectral anchoring is strictly better than point anchoring at resisting the specific deformations it targets, but it creates a new fragility: the geometry of the anchor basis itself needs to be maintained, and under sparse rehearsal you lack the data to do that faithfully beyond the first few tasks.

There is a theoretically coherent regime where new-task manifold structure could correct old-task geometric debt, but it requires a condition that is rarely satisfied in practice: the new task's embedding manifold must share enough geometric overlap with the old-task regions that gradients from new-task learning exert a corrective rather than deforming force on old representations. This is essentially the premise behind backward transfer in continual learning — the empirical observation, documented in López-Paz & Ranzato's GEM paper (2017), that new tasks occasionally improve old-task performance — but the mechanism is poorly controlled and the geometry underlying it is not deliberately exploited by any major system. The most concrete attempt to operationalize this is via shared latent structure: if you can identify that the new task's manifold lies in a subspace that is complementary to the old-task subspace rather than oblique to it, you could in principle use new-task gradients to re-anchor old-task principal directions that have drifted — something loosely analogous to what PackNet (Mallya & Lazebnik, 2018) does structurally with weight masks, but applied to representation geometry rather than parameter allocation. The interference problem is severe and comes from two directions simultaneously: first, any corrective signal applied to old-task regions requires the optimizer to treat old-task geometric error as a loss term, which means you need to detect that drift has occurred, and under sparse rehearsal you lack the reference points to measure it accurately enough to distinguish correction from further deformation. Second, even if you correctly identify the drift direction, applying a corrective gradient during new-task training couples the two tasks' loss landscapes in ways that can create saddle points or oscillatory dynamics — Farajtabar et al.'s Orthogonal Gradient Descent (2020) shows that projecting gradients to avoid interference works only when the old and new task gradients span sufficiently different subspaces, a condition that fails when tasks are semantically related and their manifolds overlap significantly. The sharpest practical constraint is that "exploiting new-task structure for correction" requires knowing, at training time, which regions of the embedding space contain accumulated debt — and that's precisely the information you've lost by operating under sparse rehearsal, creating a circular dependency: you need dense coverage to detect drift, but you're in this regime because you don't have dense coverage.

An auxiliary generative model operating in embedding space — a VAE or normalizing flow fitted online to the stream of embeddings rather than to raw inputs — does partially break the circularity, because it can synthesize coverage of the old-task manifold without storing raw examples, and its own drift can be measured more cheaply than drift in the full encoder. This is the core idea behind generative replay systems like DGR (Shin et al., 2017) and its embedding-space descendants, but moving the generator to embedding space rather than pixel space removes one critical self-correcting property: in pixel space, a generative model that drifts produces visibly degraded samples that are easy to detect and flag, whereas in embedding space, a drifted generator can produce geometrically plausible-looking embeddings that are silently off-manifold in ways that neither a human nor a simple reconstruction loss will catch. The failure modes specific to embedding space operation cluster around three problems: first, manifold conflation, where the generator learns a smoothed average of sequential embedding distributions and fills in the gaps between old-task clusters with synthetic points that never existed in any real distribution, effectively hallucinating false geometric continuity that suppresses the fragmentation signal you were trying to detect; second, mode complexity mismatch, where embedding distributions for vision tasks typically have 10–50 meaningful modes but normalizing flows and VAEs optimized for likelihood will over-represent high-density regions and under-represent sparse boundary regions — exactly the inter-cluster geometry that matters most for detecting fragmentation; third, compounding approximation error, where the generator is itself updated continually and its approximation error accumulates across tasks, so by task 10 the synthetic embeddings it produces may reflect a mixture of the true old-task geometry and its own training artifacts, with no clean way to separate signal from generator noise. Empirically, Lavda et al. (2018) and follow-on work show that generative replay quality degrades measurably after 5–8 sequential tasks even in pixel space; in embedding space the degradation is faster because the generator receives no gradient signal from the downstream task loss and has no perceptual grounding to constrain its drift. The deeper problem is that training the generator online means it is subject to the same non-stationarity as the encoder it's meant to monitor — if the encoder drifts, the generator's training signal drifts with it, so the generator chases a moving target and its approximation of the old-task distribution becomes a lagged, smoothed, and increasingly fictional version of where those embeddings actually were.

Freezing encoder snapshots at task boundaries does break the co-drift problem cleanly — a frozen encoder is a stable reference frame, so the generator trained against it is approximating a fixed distribution rather than a moving one — and this is essentially the architecture of systems like EWC++ combined with knowledge distillation (Buzzega et al., 2020), where a frozen "teacher" encoder constrains the live encoder's drift. The storage crossover calculation is straightforward and damning: a ResNet-18 encoder is roughly 45MB, a modest VAE or normalizing flow in embedding space runs 5–15MB, so a snapshot-plus-generator pair costs ~50–60MB per task boundary; a rehearsal buffer storing 200 raw 32×32 RGB images (the typical iCaRL budget for CIFAR-100) costs about 2.5MB, meaning the snapshot approach exceeds the raw rehearsal budget after roughly 1–2 task boundaries, before it has even demonstrated any geometric advantage. You can compress snapshots aggressively — quantizing to int8 cuts encoder storage to ~11MB, and parameter-efficient methods like storing only LoRA deltas from a shared backbone can bring per-task overhead to 1–3MB — but this reintroduces approximation error into the reference frame you were relying on being exact, partially undermining the co-drift fix. The more interesting implication is that the crossover point depends critically on what you're rehearsing: if raw inputs are high-dimensional (ImageNet-scale, 224×224, ~150KB per image), the snapshot approach becomes relatively more efficient, and at roughly 5–10 task boundaries with ImageNet-scale data a snapshot archive is cheaper per unit of geometric coverage than a proportionally sized raw buffer. The fundamental tension the calculation reveals is that snapshot-based methods are paying a fixed cost per task (the encoder size) while rehearsal buffers pay a fixed cost per sample — so snapshot methods scale better when tasks are few and data is high-dimensional, but deteriorate rapidly in long-task-sequence regimes (50–100 tasks, as in Split-miniImageNet benchmarks) where the fixed-per-task cost accumulates past any reasonable memory budget. What this implies architecturally is that no single mechanism — point anchors, spectral anchors, generative replay, or snapshots — is uniformly efficient across the (task sequence length) × (input dimensionality) × (rehearsal budget) parameter space, and the field's tendency to benchmark on short sequences (10–20 tasks) has systematically obscured the regimes where each approach's cost structure breaks down.

A principled switching policy exists in theory and looks like an online model selection problem: at each task boundary, you estimate the marginal geometric protection gained per byte by each mechanism given current sequence length, input dimensionality, and observed drift rate, then allocate your fixed memory budget accordingly — this is structurally identical to the bandit-style resource allocation in meta-continual learning systems like OSAKA (Caccia et al., 2021), which learns to allocate adaptation capacity across tasks online. The critical observable that makes switching tractable without future knowledge is drift velocity: if you maintain a small fixed probe set (even 20–50 points per old task) and track how fast their embedding distances to their task centroid are changing, you get a noisy but usable signal about whether the current regime favors snapshot anchoring (high drift velocity, low task count) or rehearsal (low drift velocity, high task count, high-dimensional inputs) — this requires no lookahead, only a running estimate of a quantity you can measure now. The lookahead problem is real but partially solvable via task similarity estimation: if incoming data is distributionally similar to past tasks (measurable via maximum mean discrepancy or embedding-space overlap before committing to a full training step), you can predict that future tasks are likely to exert corrective rather than deforming pressure on old manifolds, which shifts the cost-benefit toward lighter anchoring — but this estimate is only reliable in structured domains like class-incremental learning on natural images, not in genuinely non-stationary streams where task identity is undefined. The deeper issue is that switching policies have their own memory and compute overhead, and any policy that maintains per-task drift statistics is implicitly storing a compressed representation of task history — Prabhu et al.'s MIR (2020) shows that even lightweight importance-scoring for rehearsal selection adds 10–15% training overhead, and a full switching policy with drift tracking would likely add more. Where the approach breaks down entirely is at distribution shift discontinuities — abrupt shifts where a new task is structurally unlike anything seen before — because drift velocity gives you no warning before the shift, only evidence after the first gradient steps have already deformed the old manifold, meaning the switching policy is always at least one task boundary late in the worst-case regime it most needs to handle. The honest answer is that a truly online switching policy can be principled and approximately optimal in smooth or structured non-stationarity, but in adversarial or highly discontinuous streams it degrades to reactive damage control rather than proactive geometric preservation, and the gap between these two regimes is exactly where real-world deployment data tends to live.

Gradient alignment monitoring is theoretically sound as an early warning signal and is already implicit in GEM and A-GEM (Chaudhry et al., 2018), which check the sign of the dot product between new-task gradients and rehearsal buffer gradients before each update — negative dot product means the new task is actively harming old-task performance, which is exactly the geometric deformation signal you want to catch early. The statistical reliability question has a concrete answer rooted in the geometry of high-dimensional gradient spaces: gradient vectors in typical ResNet-scale models live in spaces of 10⁶–10⁷ dimensions, and the cosine similarity between two random high-dimensional vectors concentrates tightly around zero, meaning even small true misalignment signals are detectable with relatively modest batch sizes — rough calculations using concentration inequalities suggest that batch sizes of 64–128 are sufficient to distinguish genuine misalignment (cosine similarity < -0.1) from noise at p < 0.05 in gradient spaces above ~10⁵ dimensions, which is reassuring. The catch is that you're not comparing two random vectors — you're comparing a mini-batch gradient (noisy, computed over 32–128 samples) against a rehearsal buffer gradient (also noisy, computed over a typically smaller buffer), and the noise in both estimates is correlated with the loss landscape curvature, meaning your misalignment detector has elevated false positive rates precisely in high-curvature regions of the loss landscape, which are also the regions where new tasks tend to arrive and where you most need the detector to be reliable. Empirically, Farajtabar et al. (2020) and Lopez-Paz's original GEM analysis show that gradient alignment checks add roughly O(P) compute per step (P = parameter count) for the dot product, which is acceptable, but the false positive rate at batch size 32 is high enough that naive implementations trigger protective interventions on 20–30% of normal within-task batches, flooding the signal with noise. The minimum batch size for reliable detection scales with the dimensionality of the relevant gradient subspace rather than the full parameter space — if you project gradients onto the top-k PCA directions of recent gradient history (as in PCGrad, Yu et al., 2020), you can reduce the effective comparison space to k~50–200 dimensions, which makes reliable detection achievable at batch sizes of 16–32 but requires maintaining a running PCA of gradient history that itself costs memory and compute. The fundamental implication is that gradient alignment monitoring is a viable early warning system only if you accept either large batch sizes (128+, which conflicts with online learning constraints) or gradient projection (which adds architectural complexity and its own approximation errors), and in truly low-batch online regimes the detector's statistical power degrades to the point where it fires too late to be meaningfully earlier than drift velocity measurement.
